newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus peace deal hangs in balance.
newsitem.headline: Belarus peace deal hangs in balance.

text.p: A compromise deal mediated by Russia to defuse the political crisis in Belarus hung in the balance on Friday as parliament dithered over approving the deal and neither side in the row seemed ready to down swords.

After hours of angry debates, shouting and an ultimatum by President Alexander Lukashenko to approve the agreement by 6 p.m. (1600 GMT), deputies by mid-evening were still arguing over the peace pact.

There were clear signs that the deal, signed at break of dawn by Lukashenko, Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and parliament speaker Semyon Sharetsky but attacked as a sellout by opposition deputies, could be under serious strain.
Lukashenko cast doubt on his side of the deal, which was to make a November 24 referendum in which he is trying to widen his powers advisory rather than legally binding.
"As the head of state I will do my utmost to make the people's will mandatory," he defiantly told the chamber, adding after a pause: "But within the framework of the deal."

Sharetsky and constitutional court chief Valery Tikhinya agreed they would drop impeachment proceedings against Lukashenko which began after more than 70 deputies handed in a list of signatures to the court.
But by late on Friday only seven deputies had withdrawn their signatures, and other judges on the court said he had no right to sign a political agreement.
Tikhinya told Reuters the court had suspended its consideration of the case against Lukashenko but would renew it if parliament asked it to do so.
"The compromise is not ideal. We had to choose the lesser of two evils. If the president had gone on with a mandatory referendum it would have had bad consequences," he said.
In Moscow, the Kremlin trumpeted it as a political masterstroke. "I consider this to be a big victory," said President Boris Yeltsin, adding the conflict could have ended in violence.
But in Minsk, tempers rose in parliament and one pro-Lukashenko deputy tried to grab the microphone as opponents of the president denounced Sharetsky for signing the deal.

Sergei Kalyakin, head of the communist group, said the agreement suited nobody 100 percent and would have to win the approval of two thirds of parliament to be valid. "We have only gone half way. In fact there is no agreement," he said.
Social democrat deputy Pavel Znavets said parliament should press on with its bid to remove Lukashenko from office: "We must declare impeachment. God has given us one last chance."
Parliamentarians had already offered their main concession -- dropping the impeachment proceedings -- earlier in the week.
But Lukashenko, confident of popular support in Sunday's voting, had refused point blank to make terms and threatened to dissolve parliament and the constitutional court.
Chernomyrdin said that a political treaty signed between Russia and Belarus last April meant that Moscow felt closely connected to the fate of its neighbour.

Further proof of Moscow's powerful leverage over Lukashenko came on Friday when his chief aide Vladimir Zametalin told Reuters that Belarus had completed the handover of its former Soviet nuclear missiles to Russia.

The handover of the last batch of 16 missiles was due by the end of 1996, but Lukashenko suggested this month that it be delayed in order to extract a promise from NATO that it would not deploy nuclear missiles on the territory of new member states such as Poland. Moscow quickly vetoed the idea.
Under the terms of the deal a constitutional committee with 50 representatives each of parliament and of the president will draw up a new constitution over the next three months.
Headed by Lukashenko, it will base its decision on the referendum results. As things stand, the president will have a clear majority on the commission.
